The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 114, verses 1–6:

In this surah, Allah describes the attributes through which refuge is sought from the evil mentioned in this surah.

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ (113:1). Among the meanings of falaq is daybreak, and another meaning is "creation," in the sense that everything from which existence and life burst forth. As stated in Surah al-An'am (95): ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living﴾ (6:95). And in the next verse (96) it says: ﴿He is the splitter of the dawn; He has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning﴾ (6:96).

If falaq is taken to mean daybreak, the meaning is: the Lord of the dawn who, by spreading light, protects everything from the evil that is hidden in darkness. And if falaq is taken to mean creation, the meaning is: I seek refuge in the Lord of creation, who gives protection from the evil of His creatures. Thus, in both cases the meaning harmonises with the following phrase.

﴿From the evil of what He has created﴾ (113:2): from the evil of everything He has created, that is, from the evil of all creation in general and in summary. When some of Allah's creatures come into contact with others, this contact sometimes produces evil, while in some circumstances the meeting and contact of creatures produces good and benefit. Therefore, it is taught to seek refuge from the evil of creation so that only good remains. And Allah, the Creator of these creatures, is able to guide them to a path and make such arrangements that good emerges from them and evil does not appear.

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it spreads﴾ (113:3). Ghasiq literally means one who pours forth, and waqab refers to the hole in a mountain from which water flows. Here ghasiq means the night, that is, the night and what is found in it, the time when it bursts forth and spreads over the earth. The night itself is frightening, and its fear increases at a time when every hidden and unknown danger may be faced in it: for example, a savage beast may attack, a thief may break in, a deceitful enemy may strike, a poisonous insect or snake may bite. Then, at night, thoughts and whisperings attack a person; pains and sorrows come to mind; the pressure of feelings, desires and inclinations is at its height, all satanic forces are unleashed, evil signs come from every side, and human desire is at its peak at night. In short, every apparent and hidden calamity attacks at night, because darkness then prevails.

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ (113:4). Who are the blowers in knots? They are sorceresses who afflict people by bewitching the senses, who deceive the nerves, give suggestions to the human self and affect the human consciousness, who tie knots in threads and blow upon them, as is the habit of sorcerers.

Magic cannot change the reality and essence of things, nor can it create a new reality. However, a imaginative state overtakes the perception and consciousness, in the way the sorcerer wishes. As the Qur'an depicts in the story of Musa (peace be upon him) in Surah Ta-Ha (65 to 69): ﴿They said: "O Musa, will you throw first, or shall we be the first to throw?" He said: "No, you throw." Then suddenly their ropes and staffs, by the power of their magic, appeared to Musa as if they were moving, and Musa felt fear within himself. We said: "Do not fear; indeed, you will be the superior. Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made. What they have made is only a magician's trickery, and a magician never succeeds, wherever he comes from."﴾

Their ropes and staffs had not actually become snakes. Rather, Musa (peace be upon him) and the people thought that these ropes and staffs were snakes, to the extent that Musa (peace be upon him) felt fear within himself and there was a need for Allah to reassure him. But the realities became evident when the staff of Musa actually turned into a serpent and swallowed their ropes and staffs.

This is the reality of magic, and we should accept it as such. In this way, magic affects people and, according to the sorcerers' signals, influences people's senses. It creates fear in human psychology and consciousness and afflicts people, and human senses turn towards wherever the sorcerer wishes. Enough has been said here to explain the reality of sorcery and the meaning of blowing into knots. This is an evil from which Allah has commanded us to seek refuge, and to enter into Allah's protection.

Some narrations, though not all of them mutawatir but sound, state that Labid ibn al-A'sam, a Jew, cast a spell upon the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. Some narrations say its effect lasted for a few days, and others say it lasted for several months, to the extent that he would think he had gone to his wives when he had not gone, and at times he would feel he had done something when he had not done it, as some narrations state. Then these surahs were revealed for the purpose of identifying that magic and for exorcism, and when the object of magic was brought and these surahs were recited over it, the knots were untied and the bad effect ended, as some narrations state.

However, these narrations contradict the fundamental belief in the infallibility of the Prophets, that he is free from error in all his actions and in conveying the message. Our belief is that his sayings and actions are Sunnah and Shari'ah. These narrations also conflict with this. Moreover, the Qur'an explicitly refuted the allegation that he had been bewitched, because the polytheists used to claim that someone had cast a spell on him, which is why he said such things. Therefore, in our view these narrations are improbable. Furthermore, beliefs cannot be established by a single report (khabar wahid). The source of beliefs is the Qur'an, and beliefs are established from hadith only when they reach the level of tawatur, and the narrations to which we have alluded are not mutawatir. Moreover, the preferred view is that these surahs were revealed in Makkah, which further weakens the basis of these narrations.

﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾ (113:5). Envy means that, seeing Allah's bounty upon His servants, one takes a bad impression and wishes that the blessing of Allah be removed from that servant. Whether or not, after this impression, the envier strives to remove the blessings from that servant, or stops at the mere mental impression, since after this impression it is possible that he may also take some evil action against that servant.

Some secrets of this universe, some mysteries of the human self and some secrets of the human body are such that our knowledge about them is still incomplete. Therefore we should not very strongly deny them. Some mysterious events occur in these fields and we cannot reach their essence. For example, the process of transmission of thoughts over a distance, when a connection is established between two persons. Reports of such connections are coming in so frequently that one cannot doubt them, since many experiments have been made and are being made on them, and we have no reasonable explanation for the information available to us. For example, magnetic hypnotism (tanwim), which is being repeatedly tested today, but no one knows its secret. Apart from the transmission of thoughts over a distance and magnetic hypnotism (hypnotism), there are many functions of the human body and human psychology whose depths man has not yet reached.

If the envier strives and transmits this impression as an evil to that person, we cannot deny the transmission of this influence merely because, according to our knowledge and our instruments of experiment, we have not yet understood the mechanism of that transmission. This is because our information about the human self is still elementary, and the little knowledge we have obtained has been obtained only by chance. Giving it the form of a established reality remains yet to be done.

In any case, the envier's evil exists, and one should seek refuge in Allah from it and enter oneself into Allah's protection. It is Allah's grace and kindness that He guides His Messenger to seek refuge in Him, and through him the whole Ummah that comes after him is guided to seek refuge in Allah too, who provides shelter from every kind of evil.

Imam al-Bukhari, with his chain of narration, reported from Hadrat A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that when the Prophet ﷺ went to bed at night, he would join his two palms, then blow into them after reciting ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (112:1) and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ (114:1). Then he would pass his palms over the whole body, as far as possible, beginning with the head and face, and over the front part of the body as much as he could, and he would do this three times. (This hadith has been narrated by the compilers of the Sunan in this manner.)

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 114, verses 1–6:

In this surah, Allah describes the attributes through which refuge is sought from the evil mentioned in this surah.

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ (113:1). Among the meanings of falaq is daybreak, and another meaning is "creation," in the sense that everything from which existence and life burst forth. As stated in Surah al-An'am (95): ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living﴾ (6:95). And in the next verse (96) it says: ﴿He is the splitter of the dawn; He has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning﴾ (6:96).

If falaq is taken to mean daybreak, the meaning is: the Lord of the dawn who, by spreading light, protects everything from the evil that is hidden in darkness. And if falaq is taken to mean creation, the meaning is: I seek refuge in the Lord of creation, who gives protection from the evil of His creatures. Thus, in both cases the meaning harmonises with the following phrase.

﴿From the evil of what He has created﴾ (113:2): from the evil of everything He has created, that is, from the evil of all creation in general and in summary. When some of Allah's creatures come into contact with others, this contact sometimes produces evil, while in some circumstances the meeting and contact of creatures produces good and benefit. Therefore, it is taught to seek refuge from the evil of creation so that only good remains. And Allah, the Creator of these creatures, is able to guide them to a path and make such arrangements that good emerges from them and evil does not appear.

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it spreads﴾ (113:3). Ghasiq literally means one who pours forth, and waqab refers to the hole in a mountain from which water flows. Here ghasiq means the night, that is, the night and what is found in it, the time when it bursts forth and spreads over the earth. The night itself is frightening, and its fear increases at a time when every hidden and unknown danger may be faced in it: for example, a savage beast may attack, a thief may break in, a deceitful enemy may strike, a poisonous insect or snake may bite. Then, at night, thoughts and whisperings attack a person; pains and sorrows come to mind; the pressure of feelings, desires and inclinations is at its height, all satanic forces are unleashed, evil signs come from every side, and human desire is at its peak at night. In short, every apparent and hidden calamity attacks at night, because darkness then prevails.

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ (113:4). Who are the blowers in knots? They are sorceresses who afflict people by bewitching the senses, who deceive the nerves, give suggestions to the human self and affect the human consciousness, who tie knots in threads and blow upon them, as is the habit of sorcerers.

Magic cannot change the reality and essence of things, nor can it create a new reality. However, a imaginative state overtakes the perception and consciousness, in the way the sorcerer wishes. As the Qur'an depicts in the story of Musa (peace be upon him) in Surah Ta-Ha (65 to 69): ﴿They said: "O Musa, will you throw first, or shall we be the first to throw?" He said: "No, you throw." Then suddenly their ropes and staffs, by the power of their magic, appeared to Musa as if they were moving, and Musa felt fear within himself. We said: "Do not fear; indeed, you will be the superior. Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made. What they have made is only a magician's trickery, and a magician never succeeds, wherever he comes from."﴾

Their ropes and staffs had not actually become snakes. Rather, Musa (peace be upon him) and the people thought that these ropes and staffs were snakes, to the extent that Musa (peace be upon him) felt fear within himself and there was a need for Allah to reassure him. But the realities became evident when the staff of Musa actually turned into a serpent and swallowed their ropes and staffs.

This is the reality of magic, and we should accept it as such. In this way, magic affects people and, according to the sorcerers' signals, influences people's senses. It creates fear in human psychology and consciousness and afflicts people, and human senses turn towards wherever the sorcerer wishes. Enough has been said here to explain the reality of sorcery and the meaning of blowing into knots. This is an evil from which Allah has commanded us to seek refuge, and to enter into Allah's protection.

Some narrations, though not all of them mutawatir but sound, state that Labid ibn al-A'sam, a Jew, cast a spell upon the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. Some narrations say its effect lasted for a few days, and others say it lasted for several months, to the extent that he would think he had gone to his wives when he had not gone, and at times he would feel he had done something when he had not done it, as some narrations state. Moreover, the preferred view is that these surahs were revealed in Makkah, which further weakens the basis of these narrations.
